courses.title: Digital Confidence to Computer Operator
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Hands on a real keyboard: create, copy, and recover a folder tree without a mouse.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Operator confidence is not 'being good with computers.' It is knowing which of three jobs you asked the machine to do: remember (files), calculate (apps), or talk (network). Beginners freeze when a window disappears because they cannot name the job that failed.
courses.worked_example: Say the path out loud: Documents/waike/lab1. If that folder is missing, create it before copying. The lab marks missing paths — extras on the Desktop are clutter, not success.
courses.assignment:
1) Create the required tree and screenshot or list it (`ls` / File Explorer).
2) Write a 4-line operator journal: remember / calculate / talk / what broke.
3) Restore the deleted note without using Undo as your only method.
courses.lab_hint: Hands on a real keyboard: create, copy, and recover a folder tree without a mouse.

courses.title: IT Support and Hardware Foundations
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Open a (virtual) ticket, name the failing subsystem, and pick the swap part.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A ticket is a promise to restore someone's work, not a chat thread. Hardware foundations start at power, then storage, then memory, then the OS. Swapping parts before naming the subsystem is how labs waste DIMMs.
courses.worked_example: If apps crash on a 4 GB machine, add or reseat RAM before you blame the OS.
courses.assignment: Triage three tickets (boot / crash / fan). For each: subsystem, whether to swap now, and one log you would collect. No vendor names required.
courses.lab_hint: Open a (virtual) ticket, name the failing subsystem, and pick the swap part.

courses.title: Software Builder Zero-to-Hero
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Write a tiny function, run its checks, and ship a README that a stranger can run.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Shipping is smaller than 'becoming a developer.' A stranger must run what you wrote. That means a function with checks, a README with one command, and no secrets in the repo.
courses.worked_example: 49 is Retry. 50 is L. Off-by-one on the boundary is the usual bug.
courses.assignment: Implement band() for the four thresholds. Add one extra failing score. Document the run command in README. Do not copy a cooking analogy.
courses.lab_hint: Write a tiny function, run its checks, and ship a README that a stranger can run.

courses.title: Networking and Internet Infrastructure
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Compute a subnet's network address and usable hosts from a CIDR on paper then in code.
courses.lesson_excerpt: An IPv4 address is 32 bits wearing dots. CIDR steals high bits for the network and leaves the rest for hosts. /26 means 6 host bits — 64 addresses, 62 usable if you still believe in network and broadcast addresses.
courses.worked_example: /26 leaves 6 host bits. 2^6=64 addresses; usable is 62 when broadcast exists.
courses.assignment: Compute network and usable hosts for 192.168.10.40/26 and one /28 of your choice.
courses.lab_hint: Compute a subnet's network address and usable hosts from a CIDR on paper then in code.

courses.title: Cybersecurity Foundations and SOC Readiness
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Triage a fake auth log: count bursts, never paste secrets, write a one-line incident note.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A SOC junior does not 'hack back.' They count, threshold, and write one honest sentence. AUTH_FAIL lines that pile onto one user are a burst. Bursts are not proof of an attacker — they are proof you should look.
courses.worked_example: No. ada crossed the threshold; your note should say 'burst,' not 'attacker.'
courses.assignment: Write a 3-sentence incident note from the fixture. Name burst users. No secrets.
courses.lab_hint: Triage a fake auth log: count bursts, never paste secrets, write a one-line incident note.

courses.title: Data, Databases, and Dashboards
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Fold a CSV into a top-N table you could pin on a Gary lab wall.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A dashboard that cannot be rebuilt from a CSV is decoration. Start with group-by and top-N. Gary logged 20 lab hours, Ghana 5, Geelong 9 — the wall chart should match the arithmetic, not a designer’s guess.
courses.worked_example: Sum hours first. Gary is 12+8=20 and should lead the top-N.
courses.assignment: Recompute top-2 site hours by hand. Change top_n to 3 and explain what appears.
courses.lab_hint: Fold a CSV into a top-N table you could pin on a Gary lab wall.

courses.title: AI/ML and Edge AI Foundations
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Classify 2-D samples with 1-NN on-device — no cloud round trip.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Edge AI in this seed is 1-nearest-neighbor in 2-D. No GPU, no cloud, no 'training pipeline.' You store a few labeled points and assign each query the label of the closest training point by squared Euclidean distance.
courses.worked_example: (1.9,2.1) sits next to (2,2) signal. (0.1,0.2) sits next to noise at the origin.
courses.assignment: Classify two queries by hand against the three training points, then run the lab.
courses.lab_hint: Classify 2-D samples with 1-NN on-device — no cloud round trip.

courses.title: Embedded Systems and Device Prototyping
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Turn a pin list into a GPIO bitmask and explain why pin 0 is special.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A GPIO bitmask is a set of pins encoded as bits. Pin 3 set means OR with 1<<3. Pin 0 is not 'optional' — it is bit 0, value 1, and firmware people forget it because zero looks like off.
courses.worked_example: Pins 0,3,7 → bits 1 + 8 + 128 = 137 = 0x89. If you see 0x88, pin 0 was dropped.
courses.assignment: Compute the mask on paper. Explain pin 0 in one sentence. Run the lab.
courses.lab_hint: Turn a pin list into a GPIO bitmask and explain why pin 0 is special.

courses.title: Wireless, DSP, and 6G Foundations
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Count OFDM overhead: cyclic prefix vs occupied subcarriers, then say it in one sentence.
courses.lesson_excerpt: OFDM packs many narrow subcarriers into one symbol. A cyclic prefix copies the tail onto the front so delayed copies still look circular. That prefix is not free: samples spent on CP are samples not spent on new data.
courses.worked_example: 64 FFT samples plus 16 cyclic-prefix samples. Overhead 16/80, occupancy 52/64.
courses.assignment: Compute symbol_samples, cp_overhead, occupancy, and say it in one sentence.
courses.lab_hint: Count OFDM overhead: cyclic prefix vs occupied subcarriers, then say it in one sentence.

courses.title: Project Management, Agile, and Lean Six Sigma
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Walk a sticky-note critical path; the lab computes the same length.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Critical path is the longest chain of dependent work, not the noisiest standup. Lean Six Sigma will wait; today you only add durations along predecessors.
courses.worked_example: A-B-D is 2+3+4=9. C finishes earlier, so it does not extend D beyond B.
courses.assignment: Draw the four-box graph. Mark the 9-day path. Name one task with slack.
courses.lab_hint: Walk a sticky-note critical path; the lab computes the same length.

courses.title: Game Development and Interactive Media
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Move two AABBs until they overlap, then resolve the minimum translation vector.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Axis-aligned bounding boxes are rectangles that do not rotate. They overlap when they overlap on X and on Y. The minimum translation vector (MTV) is the smallest push that separates them — usually along the shallower axis.
courses.worked_example: A ends at x=10, B starts at 8 → 2px on X. Y overlap is larger, so MTV is on X.
courses.assignment: Predict overlap and MTV, then run the lab. Move B until overlap is false.
courses.lab_hint: Move two AABBs until they overlap, then resolve the minimum translation vector.

courses.title: 7GC AI-RAN Research Apprenticeship
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Compute Shannon capacity for a toy RAN slice and write the assumption list.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Shannon capacity C = B log2(1+SNR) is an upper bound under AWGN, not a 7GC field measurement. A 1 MHz slice at SNR=3 linear yields about 2 Mbit/s. Real RAN overhead, scheduling, and hardware make that number optimistic.
courses.worked_example: 1e6 * log2(1+3) ≈ 2.0 Mbps. That is a bound, not a campus measurement.
courses.assignment: Compute C. Write four assumptions. State one reason a drive-test would differ.
courses.lab_hint: Compute Shannon capacity for a toy RAN slice and write the assumption list.

courses.title: Cloud and DevOps
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Reject a broken service manifest before it reaches a cluster.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Clusters forgive nothing you forgot to reject at the gate. A class manifest needs an image with a tag, a positive replica count, a legal port, and no privileged flag. Privileged containers are forbidden in this classroom cluster even if a blog said they are 'easier for hardware.'
courses.worked_example: A passing fixture has image:tag, replicas≥1, port in 1–65535, privileged false.
courses.assignment: Break the fixture four ways (tag, replicas, port, privileged) and record errors.
courses.lab_hint: Reject a broken service manifest before it reaches a cluster.

courses.title: Communication, Professional Development, and Ethics
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Redact emails and phones from a peer draft without changing the meaning.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Professional writing in WAIKE is specific and kind, and it does not leak PII. Emails and US-style phone numbers in a peer draft get replaced with [EMAIL] and [PHONE] so a screenshot can leave the room.
courses.worked_example: Keep 'Call Maya at [PHONE] or [EMAIL] before class.' Meaning stays; digits go.
courses.assignment: Redact the fixture. Then redact a paragraph you invent that contains one email.
courses.lab_hint: Redact emails and phones from a peer draft without changing the meaning.

courses.title: Robotics and Control
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Take one P-controller step toward a heading; feel overshoot vs gain.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A proportional controller does one thing: delta = Kp * error. Heading 10°, target 30°, Kp=0.5 → you add 10° and land at 20°. You did not arrive yet. Large Kp overshoots; you can feel it by turning a chair too fast toward a tape mark.
courses.worked_example: error=20, delta=10, next=20. You are halfway; the controller is not a teleport.
courses.assignment: Compute the next heading. Repeat with Kp=2 and describe overshoot risk.
courses.lab_hint: Take one P-controller step toward a heading; feel overshoot vs gain.

courses.title: gunnchOS Device OS and Product Lab
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Parse a device session JSON and report honest uptime — no fake 100% claims.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Product lab honesty: uptime is stop minus start, summed. If a slide claims 100% and the sessions say 90 seconds in a longer window, the slide is wrong. This course sits on gunnchOS device sessions — still not a claim that Device Lab visual tokens are earned here.
courses.worked_example: Only if stop-start covers the whole window. The fixture totals 90 s, not 'always up.'
courses.assignment: Compute total and mean uptime. Invent a dishonest claim and show the lab flags it.
courses.lab_hint: Parse a device session JSON and report honest uptime — no fake 100% claims.

courses.title: Hardware Engineering
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Build a voltage divider on paper, then let the lab check Vout.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A voltage divider is two resistors in series. Vout = Vin * R2/(R1+R2) when you take the tap across R2. 5 V, 1 kΩ, 3 kΩ → 3.75 V. Current is Vin/(R1+R2).
courses.assignment: Compute Vout and current. Swap R1/R2 and predict the new Vout.
courses.lab_hint: Build a voltage divider on paper, then let the lab check Vout.

courses.title: Data Visualization and Business Intelligence
courses.kinesthetic_hook: Bin a series into a histogram you could explain to a non-engineer sponsor.
courses.lesson_excerpt: A histogram is a count of values that fell into edges. Edges [0,3,6,10] make three bins: [0,3), [3,6), [6,10]. The last bin includes the right edge so 10 does not fall on the floor. Values 1,2,2,5,9 → counts 3,1,1.
courses.worked_example: Yes for this lab. 1,2,2 land in bin 0; 5 in bin 1; 9 in bin 2 → [3,1,1].
courses.assignment: Bin the fixture by hand. Add a value of 10 and update the last bin.
courses.lab_hint: Bin a series into a histogram you could explain to a non-engineer sponsor.
